name: Congenital Vertical Talus, Unilateral

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiographic Diagnostic Criteria for Congenital Vertical Talus

criteria.description: Rigid dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus
Fixed plantar-flexion of the talus bone
Prominent calcaneus visible on lateral foot radiographs
Rigid rocker-bottom foot deformity with limited passive correction

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of rigid dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus with radiographic confirmation of talonavicular dislocation and fixed plantar-flexion of the talus
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by radiographic imaging; unilateral involvement distinguishes it from bilateral forms.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Rigid dorsal dislocation of the navicular bone
searchTerms: fixed backward dislocation of navicular bone
dorsal navicular bone fixed out of place

pathognomonic.symptomName: Fixed plantar-flexion deformity of the talus
searchTerms: foot stuck in downward pointed position

common.symptomName: Limited passive dorsiflexion of the ankle

searchTerms: prominent heel bone felt at back

common.symptomName: Unilateral foot deformity with normal contralateral foot
Abnormal gait pattern developing with ambulation
common.notes: Usually noted as child begins to walk

searchTerms: fusion of talus and calcaneus bones
one limb shorter than the other

occasional.symptomName: Secondary skin callosities over plantar surface

searchTerms: nerve and muscle problems with foot deformity

rare.symptomName: Secondary arthritis of the talonavicular joint
searchTerms: pain and swelling in foot joint

rare.symptomName: Skin ulceration due to pressure points
searchTerms: open skin wound due to pressure

imaging: Lateral foot radiographs showing dorsal dislocation of navicular on talus
other: Physical examination revealing rigid rocker-bottom foot deformity
Limited passive correction of foot position

distinguishingFeatures: Equinus and varus deformity rather than dorsal dislocation
Foot is supinated and adducted but navicular is not dislocated dorsally
Painful foot with limited subtalar motion
No fixed dorsal dislocation of navicular
Radiographs show coalition rather than dislocation

redFlags: Failure to diagnose leading to permanent foot deformity
Progressive skin breakdown or ulceration over plantar surface
Development of secondary arthritis or joint degeneration
references: Dobbs MB, Gurnett CA. Update on clubfoot: etiology and treatment. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2009 May;467(5):1146-53.
Kuo KN, et al. Congenital vertical talus: a review of diagnosis and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2012;20(6):366-74.
